objectives: Read an attention heatmap and explain what each row/column means
Derive scaled dot-product attention from first principles
Explain why scores are divided by √d_k and what breaks without it
Tune d_k in a live sandbox and see the variance blow-up yourself

slides.title: Part 1 — The one idea the whole field is built on
slides.body: Attention is the mechanism that replaced recurrence and convolution. Once you can read an attention heatmap and **derive the formula yourself**, the rest of the transformer is bookkeeping. Spend real time here.

slides.title: What attention computes
slides.body:
Look at the heatmap. Each **row is a query** (a token asking a question), each **column is a key** (a token advertising itself). Brighter = stronger attention.

Notice the row for **`are`** — almost all its weight sits on **`cats`**. The verb learned it must agree with its subject several tokens back. Nobody coded that rule; it emerged from training.

The whole point: every token gets to **look at every other token**, weighted by relevance, in a *single* parallel operation. RNNs passed information one step at a time; attention has full reach at once.

slides.title: Three vectors per token: Q, K, V
slides.body:
Each token is projected three ways:

- **Query (Q):** "What am I looking for?"
- **Key (K):** "What do I offer?"
- **Value (V):** "What information do I carry?"

The score from token $i$ to token $j$ is the dot product $Q_i\cdot K_j$ — large when query and key align. We are about to *derive* the rest of the formula rather than memorize it.

question.question: Derive scaled dot-product attention
question.goal: Starting from "each token should read a relevance-weighted blend of the others", reconstruct $\text{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{T}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$.

steps.prompt: We need a similarity score between query $Q_i$ and key $K_j$ that is cheap and rewards aligned directions. What operation?
steps.motivation: We need O(1) per pair, differentiable, and maximal when vectors point the same way — the dot product is the natural choice.
hints: It must be a single scalar per (i, j) pair.
It should grow when the two vectors align in direction and magnitude.
steps.reveal: The dot product $Q_i\cdot K_j$ is one cheap matmul for all pairs at once ($QK^{T}$) and is large exactly when query and key align.

steps.prompt: Raw scores are unbounded real numbers. We need non-negative weights that sum to 1 across keys. What turns a score vector into such weights?
steps.motivation: A convex combination of values requires weights ≥ 0 summing to 1; softmax is the smooth, differentiable map that does this.

options: ReLU then divide by the count

hints: Weights must be a probability distribution over the keys.
It must stay differentiable for backprop.
steps.reveal: Row-wise $\text{softmax}$ maps scores to a probability distribution over keys, so the output is a true weighted average of values.

steps.prompt: With d_k-dim unit-variance Q, K, the dot product variance is ≈ d_k. To keep softmax responsive, divide the scores by what?
steps.motivation: Variance ≈ d_k means std ≈ √d_k; dividing by √d_k renormalizes scores back to unit variance so softmax doesn't saturate.
hints: You want to divide by the standard deviation.
steps.reveal: Divide by $\sqrt{d_k}$: it rescales scores to unit variance, keeping softmax out of its saturated, zero-gradient regime.

steps.prompt: In one line, explain why we apply the weights to V (not to K or Q).
steps.motivation: Q and K only decide how much to attend; V is the payload — the information actually carried forward.

rubricCriteria.description: States V holds the information/content to be aggregated
Notes Q·K only determines the weights, not the content

hints: Think about which vector is the 'payload'.
steps.reveal: Q and K produce the weights; V is the content. The output is $\sum_j w_{ij} V_j$ — a relevance-weighted blend of value vectors.

question.explanation: You reconstructed every design decision: dot-product similarity, softmax for a convex weighting, √d_k for numerical stability, and V as the payload.

slides.title: Part 3 — See the √d_k effect for real

question.question: Push d_k up. Find a setting where the *unscaled* score std stays ≤ 1.5 — you can't, which is the point.
question.harnessCode:
import numpy as np
np.random.seed(0)
dk = int(d_k)
Q = np.random.randn(64, dk)
K = np.random.randn(64, dk)
s = Q @ K.T
if scale >= 1:
    s = s / np.sqrt(dk)
metrics = {"score_std": float(s.std()), "d_k": float(dk)}
question.explanation: Unscaled, std grows like √d_k (≈8 at d_k=64) — softmax saturates. Flip scale=1 and std snaps back to ≈1 at any d_k. That single divisor decides whether the layer trains.

slides.title: Why divide by √d_k
slides.body: You just watched it: with $d_k=64$ the unscaled dot product has std ≈ 8 — large scores push softmax into a near one-hot regime where gradients vanish. Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ rescales to unit variance and keeps softmax responsive. A tiny constant with an outsized effect on whether the model trains at all.

slides.title: A coreference pattern
slides.body:
Here the pronoun **`she`** attends back to its antecedent **`Maria`**. The model learned that pronouns need to know what they refer to, and attention is the mechanism that lets it look back.

In a real model this is a *circuit* spanning multiple heads and layers (Olsson et al., 2022), but the takeaway stands: trained attention discovers linguistic structure on its own.

question.question: Diagnose the failure.
question.scenario: A teammate ships an attention layer. Training loss plateaus immediately and never drops. You print the attention matrix: every row is almost perfectly one-hot from step 1. Q, K, V projections look fine.

rubricCriteria.description: Identifies missing/incorrect √d_k scaling (or otherwise over-large logits) as the cause
Explains saturated softmax → vanishing gradients → no learning
Proposes dividing scores by √d_k (or equivalent renormalization)

question.explanation: One-hot-from-step-1 + flat loss is the classic unscaled-logits signature. Variance ≈ d_k saturates softmax; its gradient is ~0 so nothing learns. Divide QKᵀ by √d_k.

hints: Q is [n, d_k], K is [n, d_k].
slides.workedSolution: Q·Kᵀ multiplies [n, d_k] by [d_k, n] → an **[n, n]** matrix. Entry (i, j) = Qᵢ·Kⱼ, the raw similarity of query i to key j. After ÷√d_k and row-wise softmax it becomes the attention-weight matrix; times V gives the [n, d_v] output.

question.question: What does the matrix product Q · Kᵀ produce?
options: An n×n matrix where entry (i, j) is the similarity score between query i and key j
A scalar — the total attention magnitude
An n-dimensional probability vector over keys
A new embedding for each token in a different space
question.explanation: Q is [n, d_k] and K is [n, d_k], so Q · Kᵀ is [n, n]. Entry (i, j) is the dot product of query i with key j — a raw similarity. After ÷√d_k and softmax (row-wise) it becomes the attention-weight matrix.

question.prompt: Explain scaled dot-product attention to your pet — in plain words, no formula. Why does every token look at every other token, and what is the √d_k for?

rubricCriteria.description: Each token reads a relevance-weighted blend of the others' information
Q/K decide the weights, V is the content
√d_k keeps the softmax from saturating so the layer can learn

slides.title: What's next
slides.body:
You derived attention from scratch, watched √d_k decide trainability, and diagnosed the classic failure. The follow-ups make it practical:

- **[Self-attention](/wiki/self-attention)** — Q, K, V from the *same* sequence.
- **[Multi-head attention](/wiki/multi-head-attention)** — many subspaces in parallel.
- **[Causal masking](/wiki/masked-self-attention)** — mask the future for autoregressive generation.

Everything important in a transformer happens in attention; the rest is plumbing around it.
